title: When Toddlers Bite and Hit
hook: Biting and hitting horrify parents, but in toddlers they're rarely about meanness — they're big feelings meeting small vocabularies. Calm, consistent responses work better than punishment.
key_points: Toddlers lash out because they have strong feelings, weak impulse control, and few words yet — it's communication, not cruelty.
Respond calmly and briefly: a firm 'No biting — biting hurts,' then turn attention to comforting the child who was hurt.
Teach the alternative: name the feeling and offer words or actions ('You're mad — say stop' or hand them a teething toy).
Prevent by spotting triggers — tiredness, hunger, overwhelm, or wanting a toy — and stepping in early. Don't bite or hit back.
content_html: Few toddler behaviors rattle parents like biting and hitting — they feel aggressive and even shameful in public. But at this age they're almost never about meanness. A toddler has huge feelings, very little impulse control, and only a handful of words, so when they're frustrated, overwhelmed, or want something badly, the feeling can come out through their hands or teeth. It's a form of communication from a child who can't yet say what they mean.
extra_html: That understanding shapes the response. Stay calm and keep it short — a firm, unfussy "No biting, biting hurts" — and then give your attention to the child who got hurt, which also makes clear that lashing out doesn't win the spotlight. Next, teach what to do instead: put words to the feeling ("You're really mad") and offer an alternative, like saying "stop," stomping, or chewing a teething toy. Most powerful of all is prevention — many incidents follow predictable triggers like tiredness, hunger, or a tussle over a toy, so stepping in early heads them off. Avoid biting or hitting back to "show them how it feels"; it only models the very thing you're trying to stop. This is general guidance — if aggression is frequent or intense, your pediatrician can help.

related.title: Why Toddlers Have Tantrums
related.hook: Tantrums are a normal part of toddler development — big feelings hitting a brain that can't yet manage them or fully put them into words.

related.title: Positive Discipline: Teaching, Not Punishing
related.hook: Discipline means teaching, not hurting. The AAP's most effective tools are calm consistency, catching good behavior, and clear consequences — and it advises against spanking and harsh words.

flashcards.prompt: Why do toddlers often bite or hit?

choices.text: Big feelings plus weak impulse control and few words — it's communication, not cruelty
Because they are deliberately trying to hurt others
Because they were not punished firmly enough

flashcards.explanation_html: Toddlers feel intensely but can't yet manage impulses or explain themselves, so feelings come out physically. It's developmental, not malicious.

flashcards.prompt: What's an effective response when a toddler bites or hits?
flashcards.back_html: Stay calm and brief ("No biting — biting hurts"), then comfort the hurt child. Help name the feeling and offer a word or action instead. Don't bite or hit back, and watch for triggers like tiredness or frustration.
